fact: Fennec foxes have very large ears that help release body heat.

Coyotes can live in deserts, grasslands, forests, and even cities.
Bobcats have short tails with dark tips and tufted ears.
Mountain lions can leap long distances with their powerful hind legs.
Desert bighorn sheep can travel across steep rocky slopes with strong hooves.
Pronghorns are among the fastest land mammals in North America.
Jackrabbits use their long ears to help release heat.
Desert cottontails rest in shade during the hottest parts of the day.
Kangaroo rats can survive with very little free water by getting moisture from seeds.
Desert woodrats build large nests from sticks and plant material.
Antelope ground squirrels can hold their tails over their backs like tiny sunshades.
Meerkats take turns watching for danger while the group searches for food.
Dromedary camels have one hump that stores fat.
Bactrian camels have two humps and can handle very cold deserts.

Oryx have long straight horns and can tolerate high desert temperatures.
Jerboas hop on long hind legs and live in sandy deserts.
Desert hedgehogs curl into a spiny ball when threatened.
Fat-tailed gerbils store extra fat in their thick tails.

Burrowing owls often live in underground burrows made by other animals.
Cactus wrens build bulky nests among thorny desert plants.
Gambel's quail have a curved plume on top of their heads.
Male sage-grouse perform special dances at gathering places called leks.
Gila woodpeckers sometimes carve nest holes into giant saguaro cacti.
Verdins build round nests with side entrances in desert shrubs.
Elf owls are among the smallest owls in the world.
Turkey vultures can find carrion partly by using a strong sense of smell.
Golden eagles use powerful talons to catch prey.
Gila monsters are venomous lizards that spend much of their time underground.
Desert iguanas can stay active during very hot weather.
Chuckwallas wedge themselves into rock cracks and inflate their bodies when threatened.
Collared lizards can run on their hind legs for short distances.

Rattlesnakes warn threats by shaking special segments at the ends of their tails.
Coachwhips are fast nonvenomous snakes found in dry open habitats.

Emus can travel long distances in search of food and water.
